hints: Start by recalling what makes any amine basic, think about what the lone pair on nitrogen must do to a proton.
Compare the structures, in which compound is the nitrogen directly attached to the ring and in which is it separated by a $\text{CH}_2$ group.
Think about how an alkyl $\text{CH}_2$ group pushes electrons versus how overlap with the benzene $\pi$ system pulls the lone pair away.
walkthrough:
Link basicity to the nitrogen lone pair**
Think like a proton. A base is a proton acceptor, so you are looking for how easily the lone pair on nitrogen can form a dative bond to $\text{H}^{+}$. The more available and electron rich that lone pair is, the stronger the base.

Place ammonia in the middle as your reference**
In $\text{NH}_3$ the lone pair is localised on nitrogen and fully available. It is your baseline. Now ask for each amine, does the organic group push more electron density onto N, or does it pull the lone pair away.

Explain why benzylamine is strongest**
In $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$ the nitrogen is not directly attached to the ring. The $\text{CH}_2$ group between the ring and N acts as an alkyl group with a positive inductive (+I) effect. It pushes electrons toward N, increasing electron density on N, so the lone pair is even more ready to bond to $\text{H}^{+}$ than in ammonia.

Explain why phenylamine is weakest**
In $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$ the nitrogen p orbital containing the lone pair overlaps directly with the benzene $\pi$ system. The lone pair is delocalised into the ring. Because it is partly pulled into the ring, it is much less available to accept a proton, so phenylamine is a much weaker base than ammonia.

Final answer: benzylamine > ammonia > phenylamine (most basic to least basic).
Basicity depends on availability of the lone pair on N to donate to / accept $\text{H}^{+}$.
Benzylamine: $\text{CH}_2$ / alkyl group has +I electron donating effect, increases electron density on N, lone pair more available.
Phenylamine: lone pair on N overlaps / is delocalised into the benzene $\pi$ system, lone pair less available.

hints: Recall the classic test for phenylamine with bromine water, what colour change and what type of precipitate is seen.
Think about how many bromine atoms substitute onto the highly activated ring and at which positions relative to $\text{NH}_2$.
walkthrough:
Recall the observation pattern**
Picture adding orange bromine water to phenylamine. Unlike benzene, no catalyst is needed. The orange colour disappears because $\text{Br}_2$ is consumed, and the trisubstituted product is insoluble in water, so you see a white precipitate.

Draw the tribromo product**
The $\text{NH}_2$ group is so activating that substitution happens three times, at the 2,4 and 6 positions (both ortho positions and the para position). Draw a benzene ring with $\text{NH}_2$ at the top and Br atoms at the two sides and the bottom, giving $\text{C}_6\text{H}_2\text{Br}_3\text{NH}_2$.

Final answer: Observations: orange / brown $\text{Br}_2(aq)$ decolourised and white precipitate formed.
Structure of M: 2,4,6-tribromophenylamine, benzene ring with $\text{NH}_2$ at position 1 and Br at 2,4,6 positions.

hints: Focus on what the lone pair on the $\text{NH}_2$ group does with the benzene $\pi$ system.
Consider how a more electron rich ring affects attack on a non-polar $\text{Br}_2$ molecule.
walkthrough:
See the NH2 group donating into the ring**
The nitrogen lone pair sits in a p orbital that overlaps with the delocalised $\pi$ system of benzene. Electrons are pushed from N into the ring, so the ring becomes much more electron rich than benzene alone.

Connect electron richness to reactivity**
Electrophilic substitution needs the ring to attack the electrophile. A more electron rich ring is a better nucleophile and can even polarise a neutral $\text{Br}_2$ molecule to create its own $\text{Br}^{\delta+}$ electrophile. That is why phenylamine reacts readily with $\text{Br}_2(aq)$ while benzene does not.

Final answer: Lone pair / p orbital on N overlaps / is delocalised with the benzene $\pi$ system.
This increases electron density of the ring, so the ring can polarise / induce a dipole in $\text{Br}_2$ more easily, electrophilic substitution occurs without catalyst.

hints: Look at where the nitrogen lone pair can go when it is next to a $\text{C=O}$ group.
walkthrough:
Spot the competing acceptor**
In benzamide, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CONH}_2$, the nitrogen is directly attached to a carbonyl $\text{C=O}$. The lone pair on N overlaps with the $\text{C=O}$ $\pi$ bond and is delocalised toward the very electronegative oxygen. Because the lone pair is tied up in this amide conjugation, it is hardly available to bond to a proton, so benzamide is a far weaker base than ammonia.
Final answer: Lone pair on N is delocalised into the $\text{C=O}$ group / across N and O, so less available to accept $\text{H}^{+}$.

hints: Identify the nucleophile and electrophile, which atom attacks the $\text{C}^{\delta+}$ of the $\text{C=O}$ group.
Recall how to show the $\text{C=O}$ bond is polar and where the curly arrow from the $\text{C=O}$ $\pi$ bond must go.
Think about what the first addition step forms, a tetrahedral species with both $\text{O}^{-}$ and $\text{NH}_3^{+}$ on the same carbon.
Consider how the intermediate collapses, which bond reforms and which bond breaks to expel chloride.
walkthrough:
Set up the nucleophilic attack**
You have neutral $\text{NH}_3$ as the nucleophile and the acyl chloride carbonyl carbon as the electrophile. Show the lone pair on N and label the carbonyl as $\text{C}^{\delta+}$ and $\text{O}^{\delta-}$ because oxygen pulls the electrons. Draw a curly arrow from the N lone pair to the $\text{C}^{\delta+}$ and a second curly arrow from the $\text{C=O}$ double bond onto O.

Draw the tetrahedral intermediate**
After addition the carbon has four single bonds: to the phenyl ring, to $\text{O}^{-}$, to Cl, and to $\text{NH}_3^{+}$. This is the organic intermediate $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{C}(\text{O}^{-})(\text{NH}_3^{+})(\text{Cl})$. Check your charges: O is negative because it gained the $\pi$ electrons, N is positive because it used its lone pair to form a new bond.

Collapse to reform the carbonyl**
Now the $\text{O}^{-}$ pushes back. Draw a curly arrow from the lone pair on $\text{O}^{-}$ to reform the $\text{C=O}$ double bond. At the same time the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond must break, so draw a curly arrow from the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond onto Cl, expelling $\text{Cl}^{-}$. This addition elimination sequence gives $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CONH}_2$ plus $\text{HCl}$ after proton transfer.

Final answer: Step 1 addition: lone pair on $\text{NH}_3$ to $\text{C}^{\delta+}$ of $\text{C=O}$ ($\text{C}^{\delta+}$ $\text{O}^{\delta-}$ shown), $\text{C=O}$ arrow to O.
Intermediate: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{C}(\text{O}^{-})(\text{NH}_3^{+})(\text{Cl})$ with correct charges.
Step 2 elimination: arrow from $\text{O}^{-}$ back to reform $\text{C=O}$, arrow from $\text{C-Cl}$ bond to Cl to give $\text{Cl}^{-}$.

hints: Think about the pH where the positive and negative charges on the amino acid exactly balance.
walkthrough:
Picture charges cancelling out**
An amino acid can be cationic at low pH and anionic at high pH. The isoelectric point is the special pH in between where it exists mainly as the zwitterion with one $\text{NH}_3^{+}$ and one $\text{COO}^{-}$, so the overall charge is zero.
Final answer: The pH at which the amino acid has no overall / net charge / exists as a zwitterion.

hints: At pH 10, well above the isoelectric point of 5.5, decide whether $\text{NH}_3^{+}$ and $\text{COOH}$ will be protonated or deprotonated.
walkthrough:
Apply high pH logic**
At pH 10 the solution is basic relative to the isoelectric point, so remove protons. Both acidic groups lose $\text{H}^{+}$: $\text{COOH}$ becomes $\text{COO}^{-}$ and $\text{NH}_3^{+}$ becomes $\text{NH}_2$. The phenyl side chain is unchanged, giving the anion $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{CH}(\text{NH}_2)\text{COO}^{-}$.

hints: Recall that a dipeptide forms by condensation between $\text{COOH}$ of one amino acid and $\text{NH}_2$ of the other, with the $\text{CONH}$ group shown displayed.
Check that either order is allowed, phenylalanine plus alanine can link in two ways, but each side of the peptide bond must join to a saturated carbon.
walkthrough:
Build the CONH link**
Join the $\text{C=O}$ from the carboxyl end of one amino acid to the NH from the amino end of the other, eliminating water. You must display the peptide group as $\text{C}(=\text{O})\text{N}(-\text{H})$, not just write CONH.

Complete either dipeptide correctly**
If phenylalanine is first, you get $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{CH}(\text{NH}_2)\text{CONHCH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{COOH}$. If alanine is first, you get $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{NH}_2)\text{CONHCH}(\text{CH}_2\text{C}_6\text{H}_5)\text{COOH}$. Both are accepted provided the free $\text{NH}_2$, free $\text{COOH}$, and side chains $\text{CH}_2\text{C}_6\text{H}_5$ and $\text{CH}_3$ are correct.

Final answer: Either $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{CH}(\text{NH}_2)\text{CONHCH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{COOH}$ or $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{NH}_2)\text{CONHCH}(\text{CH}_2\text{C}_6\text{H}_5)\text{COOH}$ with $\text{C=O}$ and N-H of peptide bond fully displayed.
